# February 29, 1960

You arrived on a Monday — and not just any Monday. You were born on a day that does not exist in most years, a date the calendar conjures only once every four years to keep itself honest with the sun.

---

## The Rarest of Beginnings

February 29 exists because a year is not quite 365 days. It is approximately 365.242 days, and without the leap year correction, our calendar would drift — seasons sliding slowly away from their months, July eventually arriving in winter. The Gregorian calendar's solution is elegant and imperfect: add a day every four years, skip it in most century years, restore it in century years divisible by 400.

You are a leaplinger — roughly one in 1,461 births. By one reckoning, you have had **sixteen** actual February 29 birthdays in your life, most recently in 2024. Your seventeenth will arrive in 2028. In the intervening years, you inhabit the small philosophical territory between February 28 and March 1, where different countries and legal traditions cannot fully agree on where you belong.

---

## The Exact Day: Catastrophe in Morocco

On the night of February 29, 1960 — the very night you were born — the coastal city of **Agadir, Morocco** was struck by a devastating earthquake. The tremor hit late in the evening local time, shallow beneath the earth and brutal in its effect. Much of the city collapsed. Approximately 12,000 to 15,000 people died, from a city of roughly 33,000. Entire neighborhoods vanished.

Morocco was a young nation — it had regained independence from France only four years earlier. King Mohammed V personally directed relief efforts. The rebuilt city that rose afterward was essentially new, its old medina gone, a planned modern city constructed in its place.

The day of your birth was a day of extraordinary destruction elsewhere in the world. That is part of the texture of the world you entered.

---

## Twenty-Eight Days Before: Greensboro

*On February 1, 1960 — twenty-eight days before you were born — four Black college students sat down at a Woolworth's lunch counter in Greensboro, North Carolina and refused to leave.*

Ezell Blair Jr., David Richmond, Franklin McCain, and Joseph McNeil were students at North Carolina A&T. They were refused service. They stayed until closing. They came back the next day with more students. Within weeks, sit-ins were spreading across the South — Nashville, Richmond, Atlanta, dozens of cities. The Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee would be founded that April.

You were born in the fourth week of a movement that would reshape the country. The Civil Rights Act, when it came in 1964, was built on actions that began twenty-eight days before your first breath.

---

## The Year on the Threshold

1960 was not quite the 1950s and not yet the 1960s we remember. Eisenhower was still president — his final year — and the country was prosperous, suburban, and deeply anxious underneath the surface. The Cold War was the permanent background radiation of daily life. The Soviet Union had launched Sputnik three years earlier; Yuri Gagarin would orbit the Earth thirteen months after you were born.

In November 1960, a 43-year-old senator from Massachusetts would be elected president by the narrowest margin in decades, and an entire tenor of American life would begin to shift. You were eight months old. The sixties, as they are remembered, were just beginning to gather.

---

## The Arc

You are 66 years old now, born into a calendar date that most people will never have as their birthday.

You were three years old when Kennedy was shot in Dallas. Nine when humans landed on the moon. Fourteen when a president resigned in disgrace. Twenty-nine when the Berlin Wall fell — an event that ended a geopolitical structure that had been the organizing fact of your entire childhood and young adulthood. You watched the internet arrive in your mid-thirties, watched it transform everything by your forties, watched a smartphone become an extension of the human hand in your late forties.

You were sixty when a pandemic shut the world down. And now at sixty-six, you are living through a moment when the tools of language and reasoning are being handed to machines.

---

## What Kind of World

February 29, 1960 was a rare day — rarer than most people's birthdays, rare enough that only a fraction of human beings share it. It was a day of earthquake and grief in Morocco, of a sit-in movement twenty-eight days old that would change the law of the land, of a Cold War running at full tension, of a world with three billion people and no human being yet in orbit.

The world your sixteen actual birthdays have witnessed since then is almost unimaginable from that Monday night. But you have been there for each transformation — which puts you in singular company, whatever date the calendar decides to call it.
